ti: Lexicon Urthus: A Dictionary of the Urth Cycle
sum: An alphabetical dictionary to the Urth Cycle (The Book of the New Sun, The Urth of the New Sun, Empires of Foliage and Flower and related short stories). Entries quote each word in context with citations, then gloss its meaning, etymology and sources: saints behind character names, mythology, archaic English, arms and armor, extinct animals, Latin terms, Gnosticism and Kabbalah. Commentary entries weigh textual puzzles. Special articles cover the calendar, history of Urth, guilds, Yesod and onomastics. The second edition adds a full character list, a narrative synopsis, maps, a subject listing and Wolfe's foreword…

ti: The Wizard Knight Companion: A Lexicon for Gene Wolfe's The Knight and The Wizard
sum: An alphabetical lexicon to The Wizard Knight (The Knight and The Wizard), with a humorous foreword by Wolfe, maps of Celidon, a cosmology diagram of the seven worlds, a chapter-by-chapter synopsis and a bibliography of myth reference works. Entries identify characters, places, weapons and peoples, cite volume, chapter and page, and give onomastic and mythological glosses drawn mainly from Norse myth and Arthuriana. Commentary entries argue specific readings, such as Ben's whereabouts when Art's letter reaches him and Black Berthold probably being a smith. The introduction notes Celidon's proto-Norse, fairy-tale culture.

ti: Gate of Horn, Book of Silk: A Guide to Gene Wolfe's The Book of the Long Sun and The Book of the Short Sun
sum: An encyclopedic companion to the Long Sun and Short Sun series, arranged as two alphabetical halves covering characters, places, gods, vocabulary and objects, with etymologies (Latin, Irish, Arabic, botany, zoology, slang), allusions (Aeneid, Odyssey, Bible, Chesterton's Father Brown), maps and timelines. Appendices treat the Whorl's languages including Tick's speech, typos, pagination concordances, and inconsistencies between Short Sun and New Sun such as Severian's age and Lune's size. The introduction recounts the project's origin on the Whorl/Urth List. Includes a foreword by Wolfe endorsing Horn as a largely reliable narrator.

ti: Gene Wolfe: 14 Articles on his Fiction
sum: A self-published collection of fourteen pieces by Andre-Driussi written between 1993 and 2014: essays, an introduction and reviews. The opening essay reads the brown book's tales in The Book of the New Sun as layered myth. It maps them onto Graves's five-part hero life and traces mythic, historical and punning sources, such as Theseus with the Monitor and Merrimack, and Romulus and Remus with Kipling and Squanto. Other pieces cover the Urth chronology, New Sun animal names, a Japanese lexicon, Fifth Head's star, Long Sun novels, and reviews.

ti: Gene Wolfe's The Book of the New Sun: A Chapter Guide
sum: A chapter-by-chapter reading guide to The Book of the New Sun, its sequel The Urth of the New Sun, and four stand-alone Urth stories, written as a companion to the author's Lexicon Urthus. Each chapter gets a brief plot synopsis followed by annotated notes on allusions and sources (Dickens's Great Expectations, Twain, Proust, Borges, Peake, Vance, Shakespeare, Clark Ashton Smith, Rex Stout, myth and the Bible), plus recurring motifs such as roses, the language of flowers, Apollo imagery and animal forms. It also records lapses in Severian's supposedly perfect memory, drawing on Urth List discussion.…

ti: Gene Wolfe’s First Four Novels: A Chapter Guide
A Chapter Guide to Gene Wolfe’s Latro Novels
A Chapter Guide to Gene Wolfe’s Smithe Novels
Between Light and Shadow
sum: A large monograph surveying Wolfe's fiction published through 1986. Part One gives extended essays on the early novels: The Fifth Head of Cerberus, Peace, The Book of the New Sun and Free Live Free. Part Two covers the short fiction and shorter novels chronologically, each entry with a summary, interpretation, allusion study and 'Unanswered Questions.' Aramini argues against postmodern readings such as Peter Wright's, holding that Wolfe's puzzles have objective solutions found through repeated symbols. For Cerberus he claims Eastwind survives in 'A Story' and that a shape-shifting Shadow child replaced Marsch.

ti: Beyond Time and Memory: An Exploration of the Fiction of Gene Wolfe 1987-1990
sum: Second volume of Aramini's multi-volume survey of Wolfe's fiction, covering 1987-1990 writing. Long thesis-driven chapters treat the Latro books (arguing Latro carries Ares/Mars within him, with gods shifting between chthonic and celestial aspects and Rome's peace preparing for Christ), The Urth of the New Sun (Yesod, Tzadkiel, the undines, Severian's ministry), There Are Doors, Pandora by Holly Hollander and Castleview. Detailed summaries and glosses follow for some twenty short stories, including Empires of Foliage and Flower, plus an appendix analysing Wolfe's poetry from For Rosemary and elsewhere.

ti: Solar Labyrinth: Exploring Gene Wolfe’s Book of the New Sun
The Long and the Short of It
Peace Indexicon
sum: A booklet-length reader's guide to Peace. Its opening essay treats the novel as a puzzle to be decoded and offers three readings. In the first, the book is young Den's prophetic dream, modelled on the China pillow tale. In the second, it is a middle-aged man's daydreams prompted by Dr. Van Ness's TAT cards, and the essay maps episodes and embedded stories onto each card. In the third, Weer is a ghost reliving his life in a purgatory-like afterlife, released when the grave elm falls. The essay is followed by character and word indexes, an…

ti: Gene Wolfe
sum: Excerpt from Gordon's monograph, chiefly its chapter on Peace. She argues the novel shows how blurry the line between mainstream and science fiction is. Its likeliest frame is a middle-aged Weer breaking down during his doctor's Thematic Apperception Test. Gordon reads the book as a character study of an isolated, guilt-ridden man and as metafiction, with embedded, unfinished stories that distance and disguise. She links Weer to Wolfe's own life and compares the novel to Proust, Borges and Dickens. The excerpt then opens a chapter on The Devil in a Forest.

ti: Attending Daedalus: Gene Wolfe, Artifice, and the Reader
sum: Book-length academic study, developed from Wright's doctoral thesis, of how Wolfe's techniques shape, manipulate and finally illuminate the reader. It opens with a bio-bibliographical overview of Wolfe's career and a survey of earlier criticism. The core analysis treats The Book of the New Sun and The Urth of the New Sun as one 'Urth Cycle', covering the underlying story, generic hybridity, steering of reader response, archaic diction, memory and textual structure, and metafictional devices. A final chapter maps the cycle against the Soldier novels and The Book of the Long Sun.

ti: Shadows of the New Sun: Wolfe on Writing/Writers on Wolfe
sum: An edited collection, introduced by Peter Wright, in two parts. Part I reprints fourteen interviews with Wolfe conducted between the 1970s and 2000s by Malcolm Edwards, Joan Gordon, Melissa Mia Hall, Robert Frazier, Colin Greenland, Nancy Kress and Calvin Rich, Elliott Swanson, Larry McCaffery, James B. Jordan, Brendan Baber, Wright himself, Lawrence Person, and Nick Gevers (one jointly with Michael Andre-Driussi and Jordan). Part II gathers Wolfe's own essays on writing, among them pieces on books within the New Sun, multivolume works, science fiction's special problems, libraries, reviewing, and reading the Bible.

ti: Self-Referentiality in Gene Wolfe's 'Seven American Nights
v: Journal of the Fantastic in the Arts
sum: Aichele argues that "Seven American Nights" is a self-referential fantasy whose identity as a text cannot be settled. He examines its three-part frame (detective's letter, Nadan's edited notebook, two women readers) and the notebook's shifting intended readers. Admitted expurgation creates a liar-paradox loop, and the drugged candy eggs make events undecidable. He traces doublings: Ardis with the dog-woman, Yasmin and Dis, drug/druj, Nadan/Ned, and significant Farsi and Arabic names. The curator's account of smell, speech and writing as abstraction frames the reading. Drawing on Todorov, Frege, Barthes and Derrida, he concludes the story undoes fantasy-as-escape…

ti: Were We Ever Innocent? Childhood Horrors of Knowledge and Sexuality in Gene Wolfe's Fiction
sum: Aramini argues that Wolfe's horror writing is undervalued and that his child protagonists are rarely innocent, caught between the pull of stories and a cruel, often violent knowledge of sex. He reads "Houston, 1943" as semi-autobiographical possession horror shaped by voodoo-Catholic syncretism, "And When They Appear" as a Christmas ghost story ending in abuse, and "Mute" as an Eden-like apocalypse with incestuous undertones. He also touches on other stories and contrasts the helplessness of Wolfe's children with the theodicy of his mature novels.

ti: Science Fictional Parabolas: Jazz, Geometry, and Generation Starships
sum: Attebery proposes 'parabola' as a term for science fiction's shared, cumulative story patterns, which combine narrative needs, scientific knowledge and commentary on the genre itself. He argues that Cawelti's idea of formula fails for sf, and draws on Delany's reading protocols, the concept of the megatext and Gary K. Wolfe's icons. His worked example is the generation-starship scenario, read mainly through Molly Gloss's The Dazzle of Day, with Wolfe and Le Guin named as later reinventors. He closes with four general features of sf parabolas.

ti: Why We Need Dragons: The Progressive Potential of Fantasy
v: Journal of the Fantastic in the Arts
sum: Baker argues from a Marxist standpoint that fantasy, often dismissed in favour of science fiction as non-cognitive and reactionary, can be a progressive, transgressive literature. Taking Jameson as an anchor and drawing on Suvin, Miéville, Lukács, Althusser, Rosemary Jackson and Pauline Johnson, he contrasts Tolkien's nostalgic, affirmative fantasy with texts that use temporal dislocation and anachronism to demystify ideology. His examples are Miéville's Perdido Street Station, Delany's Tales of Nevèrÿon and Wolfe's The Shadow of the Torturer. He concedes that Wolfe's reworked Christianity carries conservative ideas about the state, sacrifice and suffering.

ti: The Divine Irruption in Gene Wolfe’s The Book of the Long Sun
v: Logos: A Journal of Catholic Thought and Culture 11, no
sum: Beiting reads The Book of the Long Sun as Catholic allegory of divine self-revelation breaking into a closed pagan world. He argues Wolfe inverts the materialist generation-ship trope: Silk's enlightenment by the Outsider is genuine, though, like Francis of Assisi at San Damiano, Silk first misreads his mandate to save his manteion. The article contrasts the manipulative, sacrifice-hungry gods of Mainframe, the cyborg Ayuntamiento, Trivigaunte and the inhumu Quetzal with the Outsider as true God. It treats Kypris as a reflection of divine love and Silk as a Hosea- and Moses-like figure.

ti: The Divine Interregnum in Gene Wolfe's The Book of the Short Sun
v: Logos: A Journal of Catholic Thought and Culture
sum: A companion to Beiting's 2008 essay on the Long Sun, this article reads The Book of the Short Sun as depicting a 'divine interregnum': the Mainframe religion has decayed on Blue, leaving moral disorder, while faith in the Outsider is not yet established. Beiting follows Horn's quest for Silk through three religious options: restoring the old gods, turning to native powers such as the Mother and the Vanished People, or devoting himself to the Outsider. He traces Horn's self-deception after occupying Silk's body and closes on Remora's shriving, which frees Horn, and on themes of…

ti: Late Night Thoughts on Reading Gene Wolfe's The Devil in a Forest
v: Science Fiction: A Review of Speculative Literature

ti: The Fifth Head of Cerberus Reviewed
A Curiously Conflict Book: Craig Brewer Reviews Gene Wolfe’s Interlibrary Loan
A Second View of Castleview
sum: A rebuttal to Algis Budrys's negative 1991 review of Castleview, arguing the novel is far less obscure than Budrys claimed. Christopher defends its structure as an imitation of medieval French Arthurian interlacement, with chapter-ending surprise twists, then shows the Arthurian material is central. He traces the castle to the Celtic Isle and Fortress of Glass (Welsh sources, Chrétien), identifies Will Shields as Arthur returned and the hitchhiker Viviane Morgan as Morgan le Fay fused with Morgause and the Lady of the Lake, and examines Excalibur and its scabbard. He notes minor slips, such as the…

ti: Variations and Design: The Fiction of Gene Wolfe
The Book of Gold’ : Gene Wolfe's Book of the New Sun
sum: Written as the tetralogy was nearing completion, Clareson's short essay surveys The Book of the New Sun and praises it as a major achievement. He argues that Urth is built by slowly estranging a medieval-seeming setting, and that Severian's retrospective narration as Autarch, with its perfect memory, makes him a complex character, likened to Graves's Claudius. He outlines each volume's role and calls the ending open. He also notes the appendices, where Wolfe poses as a translator: this lends authority while stressing the books' fictionality, as Barth and Coover do.

ti: Some Greek Themes in Wolfe’s Latro Novels
Gene Wolfe's 'The Fifth Head of Cerberus' (1972); or, an Uncanny Science Fiction Revision of Proust's A la recherche du temps perdu: Remembrance of Things Past, Remembering Oneself
v: Etudes Britanniques Contemporaines: Revue de la Société d'Etudes Anglaises Contemporaines

ti: The Distant Suns of Gene Wolfe
v: First Things: A Monthly Journal of Religion and Public Life
sum: An overview essay in First Things introducing Wolfe as a difficult, religious writer underread even by genre fans. Farrell sketches The Book of the New Sun, treating Severian's career and the Claw as a meditation on pain pointing toward God, gives a biography covering his Catholic conversion, then concentrates on the Soldier novels, especially Soldier of Sidon, retelling its Nile plot. He reads Latro's despair as humanity awaiting the Incarnation, briefly faults There Are Doors and Castleview, and suggests the Latro books may prove Wolfe's most enduring work.

ti: Gene Wolfe and the Tale of Wonder: The End of the Apprenticeship
v: Science Fiction: A Review of Speculative Literature
sum: An appreciative essay on The Book of the New Sun as science fantasy and a tale of wonder. French outlines Urth's setting, the New Sun prophecy and Severian's journey from exiled torturer to autarch. He argues that Severian's perfect memory sustains the reader's belief, that clues identify him as the returning Conciliator in a pantheistic universe, and that the narrative works as a loop. He also praises Wolfe's archaic and coined vocabulary and the embedded tales: the Theseus adaptation, the story-telling contest, and the Ascian prisoner's story.

ti: The Rhetoric of an Impossible Object: Gods, Chems, and Science Fantasy in Gene Wolfe's Book of the Long Sun
v: Extrapolation: A Journal of Science Fiction and Fantasy
sum: Gerlach argues that science fantasy is not a stable subgenre but an unstable mixture, and that this instability drives the effects of The Book of the Long Sun. Readers first try to explain the fantasy scientifically, reading the whorl as a generation ship and the gods as computer programs in Mainframe. The theophanies still keep their mythic force, though. The chems produce comic ironies about robots, labour and sex. The Outsider gradually emerges as the God of our own world, so the key shift is ultimately from fiction to theology.

ti: Gene Wolfe’s Sleight of Hand
v: The Australian Science Fiction Review, March

ti: The Mercy of the Torturer: The Paradox of Compassion in Gene Wolfe's World of the New Sun
sum: Heldreth traces the theme of mercy across the five volumes of the New Sun sequence, arguing that Severian, unlike conventional heroes, begins in an evil profession and progressively redefines mercy: from pity for the dog Triskele, to giving Thecla the knife, to freeing Cyriaca, after which the Claw's power returns. Justice is shown as an unattainable absolute, while mercy follows organic logic. Severian moves beyond dualism toward a Buddhist-like compassion, and in Urth becomes a torturer-saviour whose New Sun both destroys and redeems Urth. The essay draws on NPR accounts of real torture and on…

ti: The Fourfold Library (4)
v: Foundation: The International Review of Science Fiction
sum: A short personal essay in Foundation's "Fourfold Library" series in which novelist Peter Higgins explains how The Book of the New Sun made him a writer. He argues that Wolfe dissolved the supposed barrier between ambitious literary fiction and commercial genre writing. Using the cliff-face strata passage from The Sword of the Lictor as an emblem, he describes the sequence as absorbing earlier fantasy writers and American narrators such as Ishmael and Huck Finn. He sets it beside encyclopaedic epics and casts Wolfe as SF's white whale.

ti: Art and Allegory: A Method to Read The Book of the New Sun by Gene Wolfe
v: Logos: A Journal of Catholic Thought and Culture
sum: Lopez argues that The Book of the New Sun is a dual text. Read by modern methods it is a secular political memoir of a rise to power; read through medieval allegorical techniques it is a Catholic conversion narrative. After surveying earlier critics (Gordon, Wright, Clute) and giving a long plot summary, she applies Singleton's "allegory by evocation" and Anglo-Saxon onomastic practice. She traces allusions to Scripture, the liturgy, Augustine and Aelred of Rievaulx. She concludes that Wolfe aims at reader conversion and calls for study of parallels with Dante's Divine Comedy.

ti: Remembering the Future: Gene Wolfe's The Book of the New Sun
sum: An essay by Peter Malekin on The Book of the New Sun, collected in a volume of papers from the Fifth International Conference on the Fantastic in the Arts (1984). The essay text itself is not in the scan. The editor's part introduction says it examines how past, present and future relate in Wolfe's tetralogy, a reading suggested by the title's idea of remembering the future. Malekin's contributor note gives his main interest as the fantastic and the theory of consciousness.

ti: Terminus Non Est: Gene Wolfe's The Book of the New Sun
sum: Manlove's study of The Book of the New Sun, first published in Kansas Quarterly (1984) and later revised as chapter 11 of his Science Fiction: Ten Explorations (1986). The book's index outlines the chapter's topics: the work's character as science fiction, its refusal to explain, how it restricts narrative drive, the nature of its imagination, its metaphysical ground, a recurring motif of reversal, identity without fixed boundaries and an inclusive vision, and how meaning works in the text. The book's wider aim is close literary attention to the invented worlds of science fiction.

ti: The Monomyth in Gene Wolfe's The Book of the New Sun
v: Extrapolation: A Journal of Science Fiction and Fantasy
sum: Palumbo reads The Book of the New Sun as a detailed reworking of Joseph Campbell's monomyth. He argues that the four volumes trace Campbell's departure, initiation and return stages roughly in Campbell's order, and that Urth repeats the pattern. Each volume also foreshadows and echoes other stages. Severian is shown to fit the archetypal hero: an orphan who unknowingly finds his father (Ouen), an exile, and a man who personifies and does not fear death. His gifts are near-perfect memory, healing and resurrection that come from himself rather than the Claw, and the torturer's equanimity…

ti: The Dialogic Science Fiction Megatext: Vivisection in H. G. Wells’ The Island of Dr. Moreau and Genetic Engineering in Gene Wolfe’s ‘The Woman Who Loved the Centaur Pholus
sum: Pak reads Wolfe's story as a deliberate dialogue with Wells's The Island of Dr Moreau, using Broderick's idea of the sf megatext. He first analyses Moreau's vivisection as a precursor to genetic engineering, covering blasphemy, pain, rationality and Prendick's fear of atavism. He then argues that Wolfe's 'life-shaping' story updates those debates with modern animal-rights and extinction concerns. Pholus is read as a figure that blurs boundaries of species, race and gender and points toward a utopian future, while Anderson stays with the dying twentieth century.

ti: The Gods Problem in Gene Wolfe's Soldier of the Mist
sum: A chapter in a Bloomsbury edited collection on classical reception in science fiction and fantasy, placed in the section on displacing genre. Judging only by its title, it addresses how the Greek gods are handled in Wolfe's Soldier of the Mist. The scan contains none of the chapter's text, so its argument and specific claims cannot be described here. The contributor note identifies Tomasso as a classicist at Trinity College, Hartford, who works on Greek epic and popular reception of antiquity.

ti: God-Games: Cosmic Conspiracies and Narrative Sleights in Gene Wolfe's 'The Fictions of the New Sun
v: Foundation: The Review of Science Fiction

ti: Grasping the God-Games: Metafictional Keys to the Interpretation of Gene Wolfe's 'The Fictions of the New Sun
v: ' Foundation: The Review of Science Fiction

ti: A Weird Mystery: James Wynn Considers Gene Wolfe’s A Borrowed Man
A Wolfe With Surface Traction: There Are Doors by Gene Wolfe
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Joan Gordon reviews There Are Doors, calling it Wolfe's most accessible novel since Operation Ares, with plain style, few characters and little allusion. She groups Wolfe's works by protagonist type and compares the book closely to Operation Ares, but sees it as a novel of character driven by myth rather than warning. She reads the plot as several simultaneous stories: lover's quest, goddess devotion, and schizophrenic fugue. She notes livelier female characters and that Green's home world subtly differs from ours. Verdict: elegant and well made, though less richly layered than The Book of the…

ti: Soldier of Arete by Gene Wolfe
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Review of Soldier of Arete (Tor, 1989). Killheffer reads the Soldier books as a mirror image of The Book of the New Sun: amnesiac Latro versus total-recall Severian, with character parallels (Eurykles/Drakaina with Talos, Baldanders and Jolenta; Io with Dorcas; Seven Lions with Jonas). He argues the series extends Wolfe's study of memory as the basis of identity, and of history as a nation's memory, flawed by perspective and gaps. Latro's darkening tone and habitual rereading are defended as consistent with the premise. Verdict: a difficult, dark but worthy sequel.

ti: Endangered But Still Vital: Endangered Species by Gene Wolfe
sum: A review of the Tor hardcover of Endangered Species, a 34-story collection with little overlap with earlier Wolfe collections. Gouvéa welcomes it as a sign that Wolfe still writes short fiction, praises its range, quality and emotional depth, and notes that the stories reward rereading though some, like "Lukora," may be opaque. He singles out the horror pieces, the narrative voice of "When I Was Ming the Merciless," and "The Detective of Dreams" as a Christian parable. He also notes science fiction stories in which characters read events in mythic terms. The verdict is strongly…

ti: Fish Whistle by Daniel Pinkwater
v: New York Review of Science Fiction

ti: Castleview by Gene Wolfe
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: John Clute reviews Castleview, framing it as a book that resists a first reading. He recounts his own halting first pass through its farcical, crowded opening, then credits Neil Gaiman with the key insight: the novel is about recruiting an Arthur, signalled by the many head wounds echoing Malory. He traces Puss in Boots allusions and compares its plain style to Free Live Free and There Are Doors. His verdict is strongly favourable: possibly Wolfe's finest and most lucid Catholic dream allegory, closely akin to Chesterton's The Man Who Was Thursday.

ti: The Evidence of Things Not Shown: Family Romance in The Book of the New Sun
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: First installment of Feeley's essay arguing that The Book of the New Sun encodes a hidden family romance behind Severian's apparently artless narration. He reads the Autarch as a maimed Fisher King and identifies Catherine, the woman at the guild feast, as Severian's mother. He weighs Merryn and the mandragora as candidates for a twin sister Severa, and identifies the four books Severian read with Thecla, using Wolfe's essay on them. He notes unnamed characters (Dorcas's husband, Jolenta's original self, the Autarch) as clues. Appendices collate chronologies implying the androgyne Autarch bore Severian with Catherine.

ti: Smiling, She Met the Dragon [on Sharon Baker]
v: New York Review of Science Fiction

ti: The New Gothic: A Collection of Contemporary Gothic Fiction
v: New York Review of Science Fiction

ti: Six Writers in Search of a Genre: Responses to John Kessel's 'The Brother from Another Planet
v: The New York Review of Science Fiction
pub: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: A letters forum in which six writers (Thomas M. Disch, Gene Wolfe, Judith Moffett, Kit Reed, Gregory Benford and Brian Attebery) respond to John Kessel's essay comparing sf and mainstream short fiction by length, tense and narrative mode. Disch mocks MFA-bred minimalism. Wolfe's short letter argues that Kessel should have tabulated the authors' academic backgrounds, and likens first-person present tense to free verse: easy to write, hard to criticize. Others discuss plotlessness in literary stories, novelty as a crutch in sf, mainstream bias against the fantastic, and how context makes conventional narration strange.

ti: Nightside of the Long Sun
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Killheffer reviews Nightside the Long Sun as proof that unapologetically genre-bound science fiction can match crossover fiction. He sets out the generation-ship setting, Patera Silk's enlightenment and his scheme to save his manteion, and the hint of a pagan-to-Christian conversion. He praises the tension between a faith that is literally true (the gods live in the ship's computer) and one that may be misguided, contrasting Card's Homecoming books. He faults the virgin/whore portrayal of women but gives a strongly positive verdict overall.

ti: Angry Candy by Harlan Ellison
v: New York Review of Science Fiction

ti: Lake of the Long Sun
v: New York Review of Science Fiction

ti: Bibliomen by Gene Wolfe
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Don Webb reviews the expanded Broken Mirrors edition of Bibliomen, a set of sketches of librarians, dealers, writers, printers and publishers framed as characters awaiting a book. He calls it a rare interlayered fiction, comparing it to Richard Horn's Encyclopedia. He judges the sketches competent, some brilliant, and humorous and slightly surreal. He notes how entries cross-reference one another, so readers must flip back and forth. Citing Kostelanetz on nonlinear fiction, he asks how such a book can be finished. He ends with the playful legend of a missing twenty-third character. The verdict is warmly…

ti: A Critic at the Crossroads: Gregory Feeley's 'How Far to th' End of the World?
v: New York Review of Science Fiction

ti: Thoughts on Gene Wolfe's Peace
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Broderick's essay reads Peace as the memory-meditation of a dead Alden Dennis Weer. He argues the opening fallen elm, Eleanor Bold's grave-tree plan, and a Necronomicon passage about a soul wandering the skull's chambers show the mnemonic house is Weer's skull. He treats the novel as a web of lies and forgeries centred on Lou Gold. He also weighs Weer's possible crimes, Doris's parentage, and Julius Smart's pharmacist tale. He reports a 1985 conversation in which Wolfe confirmed the 'weerwolfe' pun, Peacock's guilt and the Tang brand name.

ti: Tentative and Incomplete Chronology of Gene Wolfe's Peace
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: The scan does not contain the chronology named in the request. It contains Schuyler's review of the 1995 Orb reissue of Peace. The review reads Weer as a ghost whose house is a poorly planned memory palace. It argues that his life emerges through nested embedded tales, such as the princess and suitors, the marid Naranj, the Chinese pillow tale and Julius Smart's pharmacist story. From these it infers his guilt over a freezer death and Smart's drugging of Aunt Olivia. It closes with open questions, including Weer's chronology, and praises the novel.

ti: Three Dreams, Seven Nights, and Gene Wolfe's Catholicism
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Locey, writing as a practicing Catholic, argues that familiarity with Catholic theology and symbolism enriches readings of two Wolfe stories. In "The Detective of Dreams" she traces the three dreams to Matthew's parables (Wedding Garment, Unmerciful Servant) and Pilate's wife, decodes Christ and Paradise imagery, and reads the stained-glass revelation and Eucharist as sacramental encounters, noting Poe echoes. In "Seven American Nights" she argues Christian symbols (bleeding, bread, Easter eggs, eagle) signal emptiness and loss, examines Nadan's unreliable perception and Shah Namah parallels, and proposes the missing seventh night is the Easter Vigil.

ti: In Search of Lost Suzanne: A Lupine Collage
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Broderick assembles and condenses an URTH mailing-list discussion (1997-98) of Wolfe's short story "Suzanne Delage." Michael Andre-Driussi identifies its source in a passage of Proust's The Guermantes Way; others note Proustian echoes in Fifth Head and Peace. Participants debate where the story's fantastic element lies: vampirism (Suzanne 'unable to be photographed'), reincarnation, a cosmos conspiring against the pair, a repressed or screen memory, or simply bittersweet regret. Broderick adds an Ives Delage cloning association and concludes that readers rule the text, though Wolfe may outwit them all.

ti: Catherine and Beyond: A Search for Maternal Roots in Gene Wolfe's Book of the New Sun
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Borski investigates the identity and ancestry of Catherine, Severian's mother, in the New Sun books. He first rejects Clute's theory (in Strokes) that Catherine is the old autarch, citing "The Cat," which names that autarch Appian, and noting that Clute miscounted the phrases set off by ellipses. Drawing on textual clues such as her height, dark colouring, apparent agelessness and old-fashioned name, he links Catherine to Valeria and the Atrium of Time. Using Urth, he proposes that Catherine is Valeria's daughter by Caesidius, which would make Severian his own wife's grandson.

ti: Thinking about the Mandragora in Wolfe's Citadel
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Borski challenges John Clute's suggestion that the bottled mandragora Severian revives in the Citadel is his lost sister. Reading the word etymologically as man plus dragon, he links it to Typhon, the dragon of myth and a Satan figure, who he argues was originally an alien. Drawing on Echidna's fragmentary words about the prime calcula and the Citadel in Caldé of the Long Sun, he proposes the mandragora is the first chem prototype, which died when Typhon tried to possess it, and supports this with the mandragora's own statements and its alien-furnished setting.
th: links between new sun and long sun

ti: Masks of the Father: Paternity in Gene Wolfe’s Book of the New Sun
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Borski argues that the Book of the New Sun is structured around several masked father figures besides Severian's actual father Ouen, chiefly Palaemon, Father Inire and Ossipago, and that unmasking them is central to the series. He reads Ossipago as a suited alien rather than a robot, citing Wolfe's naming conventions. He proposes that Famulimus and Barbatus are the children of Inire and the Cumaean, and identifies Inire with Ossipago, the cowled servant in the House Absolute, the masked jungle shaman, and Ceryx. He closes by asking whether Severian or the Inires is the greater…

ti: Gene Wolfe's Strange Travels
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Witcover reviews the collection Strange Travelers (1999) and opens with an extended essay on Wolfe's aesthetics. He links Wolfe's engineering background and Catholic faith to his fiction, arguing that Wolfe builds stories the way God built the world, with hidden patterns left for diligent readers, and that he writes for God as well as for people. He compares Wolfe's method to Nabokov's via Brian Boyd. He then discusses "Bluesberry Jam" and "Ain't You 'Most Done?" as paired, Moebius-like frame stories, and praises "The Ziggurat" as the collection's finest story. The verdict is strongly positive.

ti: On Blue’s Waters by Gene Wolfe
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Joan Gordon's review of On Blue's Waters, the opening volume of The Book of the Short Sun, judges it magnificent and the best novel she has read in a long while, more engaging than the Long Sun books. She describes Horn's double quest for Silk and for seeds, the Odyssey parallels, and the layered frame of narration and metanarration in which the narrator admits his own unreliability. She praises the plainer, fatherly voice and the hus Babbie. Her central reading is of the book as a candid study of fatherhood and how parents fail.

ti: The Island of Doctor Death and Other Stories and Other Stories by Gene Wolfe
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Jenny Blackford reviews Orb's 1997 reprint of the 1980 collection and recommends it highly. She argues that the title signals Wolfe's recurring concerns with islands, doctors and death, and the love of stories. She notes how often the dead appear in his fiction. Most of the review is plot-revealing readings of the three linked 'Death/Doctor/Island' stories, 'La Befana', 'The Eyeflash Miracles' and 'Seven American Nights'. She finds some stories weaker on rereading, among them 'Three Fingers', 'The Toy Theater', 'Hour of Trust' and 'Cues'.

ti: In Green’s Jungles by Gene Wolfe
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: A highly favourable review of In Green's Jungles, the second Short Sun volume, which the reviewer suggests may be Wolfe's finest work. It outlines Horn's arrival in Blanko, his renaming as Incanto, the threat from Duko Rigoglio, and the spy mystery and storytelling contests at Inclito's farmhouse. It recalls On Blue's Waters' Odyssey-like frame and compares its narrative-journal structure to Soldier of the Mist. It identifies the book's concerns as stories and storytellers, fathers and daughters, Horn's growing resemblance to Silk, the inhumi, slavery and the Vanished People.

ti: Languages of the Dying Sun
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Andre-Driussi compares three 'dying sun' novels, Vance's The Dying Earth, Wolfe's Book of the New Sun and Broderick's The Black Grail, as science fantasy. He argues that each builds a 'time gulf' through its vocabulary. Vance relies on archaic and faux-archaic coinages. Wolfe pushes toward fantasy by reviving real forgotten words: mythic names, saints' names for mortals, khaibit, Yesod and Briah. He also blurs clock time and has Urth turn rather than the sun rise. Broderick reaches the science fiction limit with Russian and Japanese name layers and Arthurian myth. An appendix charts each book's…

ti: Wolves in the Fold: Lupine Shadows in the Works of Gene Wolfe
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Borski traces hidden wolf figures, many of them authorial self-insertions, across Wolfe's fiction. He decodes Number Five's real name in The Fifth Head of Cerberus as Gene Wolfe or Jean Loup. He reads Ouen, Severian's father, as a Wolfe stand-in and links Oreb in the Long Sun books to the wolf-prince Zeeb. His main argument is that Latro is an unknowing werewolf cursed by Demeter. For evidence he uses the Neurian lore, Oior and Spu, divine hints, and the lukos/leukos (wolf/light) wordplay in the names Lucius and Latro.

ti: Khaibits and Other Shadows: Looking for Severia in the Book of the New Sun
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Borski hunts for Severa, Severian's unidentified twin sister in The Book of the New Sun. He sets five criteria: same age and resemblance, a pseudonym with hagiographic echoes, a witch upbringing, possible incest with Severian, and solar or 'gold' imagery. Testing the consensus candidate Merryn, including her brief appearance in Return to the Whorl, he rejects her and argues she is an alien daughter of the Cumaean. He then makes the case for the House Azure prostitute Barbea and for Jolenta, finally proposing that both are the same woman, Severa.

ti: Queen of Shadows: Unveiling Aubrey Veil in Gene Wolfe's Fifth Head of Cerberus
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Borski examines Veil's Hypothesis, the claim that the aboriginal shapeshifters of Sainte Anne replaced the human colonists, and weighs textual evidence across all three novellas for and against it: ritual scarring, facial shape-changing, inability to use tools, and dilapidated buildings, set against the general competence with tools. He concludes that the question is deliberately left unresolvable, tied to the book's concern with identity. He then argues that Aunt Jeannine is herself Aubrey Veil and an abo. On this reading her 'girls' are Shadow-child eidolons, and a patron in the garden is the real John Marsch.

ti: Reading Gene Wolfe's Return to the Whorl
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Blackford's essay is part guide and part assessment of Return to the Whorl, which she treats as the culmination of a single long narrative running through the New, Long and Short Sun books. She urges readers to reread the whole sequence first, then recaps the plots and the links between them: Typhon as Pas, the Whorl, Silk, Horn's narration and his apparent occupation of Silk's body. She finds the book's indirection and weak closure demanding, notes its open puzzles about the inhumi and astral travel, and finds its Eucharistic religious imagery somewhat uncomfortable.

ti: The Knight at the Door
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: An email interview in which Neil Gaiman questions Wolfe about The Knight. Wolfe says he wanted a fantasy world as an eleventh-century person might have imagined it, describes his light research into medieval soldiers and horses, defines high fantasy as giving hope and courage, and explains splitting the work into two volumes. Gaiman traces Wolfe's unreliable narrators from Peace to Able. Wolfe also discusses Able's speech, favourite characters (Able, Mani, Idnn), four drafts, and the knightly ideals of honour and fidelity. The piece ends by circling back to Wolfe's opening joke answers.

ti: Two Views: The Knight by Gene Wolfe
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Paired reviews of The Knight. Person argues the book mimics generic fantasy but is far richer. He compares Able to Silk, its episodic plot to Severian's, and its elisions to Short Sun, and praises the living companions as reworked plot coupons. Danehy-Oakes calls it his most gripping read since Tolkien. He analyses the Norse-Christian cosmology, Arthurian echoes, Kulili as a chaos monster, and themes of memory, names and narration, including the Abel pun and a possible hospital-dream reading. He faults annoying lacunae, peasant dialects and the cliffhanger. Both verdicts are strongly positive.

ti: The Wizard Knight: The Knight by Gene Wolfe
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Clute reviews both volumes of The Wizard Knight, reading it as a single story and describing Wolfe's novels as steganographs, texts in which the truth is fully visible if read exactly. He outlines Able's letter to his brother Ben, his geas of love for Disiri, the sevenfold cosmology, and the debt to Yves Meynard's The Book of Knights. He argues that becoming a knight means learning to love and take responsibility. He calls Able Wolfe's most open expression of pure feeling and praises the ending as one of the greater endings in the literature. The…

ti: In Praise of David Drake
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
as: Malzberg, Barry N.; Wolfe, Gene; Hartwell, David G.
sum: Three introductions written for Night Shade Books' three-volume collection of David Drake's Hammer's Slammers military SF, printed together. Malzberg says Drake's fiction shows war flattening its participants, in the tradition of Remarque, Mailer and Heller. Wolfe, drawing on his own Korean War service, notes how few writers have been soldiers. He argues SF should explore what might be rather than predict, and sets out criteria for good SF. He also insists that combat does not dehumanize soldiers and values the friendships formed under fire. Hartwell traces Drake's marginalization as a military SF writer and reads…

ti: Pirate Freedom by Gene Wolfe
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: John Clute reviews Pirate Freedom, calling it strange, entrancing and hugely enjoyable but less rewarding to unpack, especially for readers who do not share Wolfe's Catholicism. He notes that it needs less decipherment than earlier Wolfe novels, with a unicursal maze, and finds it his angriest book. Clute summarizes the timeslip plot and the Brother Ignacio doubling. He compares the priest-pirate Chris closely with Severian: torturer, confessor, morally certain. Clute reads Chris as a self-confessed bad priest and impostor, so the novel can be taken as a warning against such models.

ti: In the Penal Colony
v: New York Review of Science Fiction

ti: The Socerer’s House by Gene Wolfe
v: New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: John Clute's review of The Sorcerer's House argues that, unusually for Wolfe, the novel can be enjoyed fully on a first reading as a jeu d'esprit. Clute surveys Wolfe's habitual use of found manuscripts and absent implied authors, and places this epistolary novel in that line. He notes its pervasive doublings and black-related names, and reads it as a godgame in which Baxter Dunn inherits Zwart Black's magical house. He hears echoes of Castleview and Citadel of the Autarch, and decides to treat the ambiguous closing chapters as camouflage. Verdict: warmly positive.

ti: Does It Mean? Gene Wolfe: Perverse Puzzle Maker
sum: Aramini's 2019 UNLV doctoral dissertation argues that authorial intention in Wolfe can be recovered. Against critics such as Adam Roberts, Peter Wright and Nick Gevers, who read Wolfe as postmodern, indeterminate or naturalistic, it casts him as a traditional, rigorous Catholic symbolist whose puzzles have determinate solutions. Chapters treat "Trip, Trap" and the Soldier books, Jungian archetypes in Castleview and The Wizard Knight, and Thomist theodicy in Urth and Short Sun. Later chapters cover intertextuality in "The Changeling," "Seven American Nights" and The Sorcerer's House, and mise en abyme in Peace, Fifth Head and Short…

ti: Transcendent Outsiders, Alien Gods, and Aspiring Humans: Literary Fantasy and Science Fiction as Contemporary Theological Speculation
sum: A 2011 Stony Brook PhD dissertation in English arguing that mainstream debate between believers and New Atheists neglects what concepts of transcendence are credible and how morality might evolve, and that literary science fiction and fantasy offer room for such speculation. Early chapters examine aliens as godlike "transcendent outsiders", both judgmental and New Age-loving. Chapter four introduces "aspiring humans" and claims that in the Wizard Knight and Short Sun books Wolfe uses such figures to probe human identity, morality and theology, ultimately offering hierarchical Christian answers.

ti: Only in story a world : atheistic metanarrative in LeGuin, Pullman and Wolfe
v: University of Richmond, UR Scholarship Repository, Honors Theses
sum: An undergraduate honors thesis arguing that Le Guin's Earthsea books, Pullman's His Dark Materials and Wolfe's New Sun books dissolve modern divisions between religion, science and magic, and offer narrative as a replacement source of meaning. The authors are taken in a deliberate order. Le Guin's priest-like wizards and her revision of her own world come first. Pullman's materialist critique of the Church follows. Wolfe comes last, collapsing the material–spiritual divide, and Severian is read as rejecting the false choice between science and faith. The thesis draws on Stanley Hauerwas's narrative ethics and treats atheism…

ti: An Examination of Gene Wolfe's The Book of the New Sun: Literary and Mythological Significance
sum: A 2016 undergraduate honors thesis in English (Bridgewater State University) that argues for the mythological and symbolic power of The Book of the New Sun, written in response to Peter Wright's naturalistic reading in Attending Daedalus, which treats deliberate authorial misdirection as its basis. Garvey links Severian's three meanings of every object to Origen's threefold scriptural exegesis. He compares the multi-voiced Autarch-narrator to the Bible's many authors and reads Dorcas and the hemisphere imagery as signs of a dual religious/rational interpretation. An appendix summarizes all five novels.

ti: A study of the major science fiction works of
v: Gene Wolfe. Degree: Image, English Language and Literature
sum: Gevers's MA thesis (University of Cape Town, 1991) argues that in the New Sun cycle, The Fifth Head of Cerberus and Soldier of the Mist, Wolfe portrays the longing to know the self and God, and how nearly impossible that knowledge is to reach. Three chapters treat the New Sun books: their religious, apocalyptic and messianic structures, their narrative devices that alternately clarify and obscure, and their metafictional subversion of genre conventions. Later chapters cover identity, Gothic and dystopian elements in Fifth Head, and the role of amnesia and inscrutable Greek gods in Soldier of…

ti: Fantasy, imagination and history : a historiographical study of J.R.R. Tolkiens's The Lord of the rings and Gene Wolfe's The Book of the new sun
sum: A University of Western Australia history PhD thesis reading Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings and Wolfe's The Book of the New Sun as 'feigned history'. It argues that fantastic world-building should be understood through the historical imagination rather than as myth-making. Tolkien is placed in Romantic anti-modern historicism. Wolfe's Urth is treated as a genre hybrid of science fiction and fantasy, read through cultural history (relics, material culture) and through post-history, memory and amnesia. Despite their differences, the thesis finds both works share a Romantic cultural-history tradition.

Cyberpunk Forum/Symposium
sum: A symposium in Mississippi Review, assembled by Larry McCaffery, in which science fiction writers give short statements on the cyberpunk movement. Visible contributors include J. G. Ballard (welcoming it), Greg Bear (calling it brilliant branding he is not part of), Gregory Benford (calling it marketing posing as a movement and an assimilation of New Wave lessons into hard SF) and David Brin (placing it in generational cycles of literary rebellion). Wolfe's closing contribution judges cyberpunk uneven, credits Gibson's skill, and treats it as SF's response to the computer-human interface.

ti: The Ogre’s Fingertip: The Tale of the Student and His Son & A preliminary to literary criticism of the works of Gene Wolfe
sum: An unpublished monograph or thesis that reprints Wolfe's embedded story "The Tale of the Student and His Son" from The Book of the New Sun and then reads it as a "true myth" in the sense used by de Santillana and von Dechend's Hamlet's Mill, encoding astronomical events such as the precession of the equinoxes and the Milky Way's Great Rift. Wynn annotates the tale's figures (Corn Maidens, the ogre, Noctua, the alfange) as celestial references. He then traces recurring motifs across Wolfe's fiction, including the tolling bell, blue and green, forgetting, and Aphrodite and…

ti: An Evil Guest: “Here’s a Coconut”
sum: A chapter on An Evil Guest that opens with Wolfe's choice to read chapters twenty and twenty-one aloud at the 2013 Nebula Awards, where he was named Grand Master. The author argues that hearing Wolfe read showed those chapters to be deliberately comic, such as the Takanga sedan-chair scene with King Kanoa. The author still finds the novel stitched together from disparate influences. The chapter asks whether its third-person narration may filter Cassie Casey's delusions as untrustworthy fact, as in "The Ziggurat" and There Are Doors. It also frames the novel around Cassie and the…

ti: By Sword and Spirit: An Exploration of the Fiction of Gene Wolfe, 1991-2003
sum: Aramini's monograph offers extended readings of Wolfe's fiction from 1991 to 2003. Long chapters cover the Long Sun and Short Sun series, followed by individual essays on roughly fifty short stories. The Long Sun chapter argues that dreams and visions reveal Silk as an embryo carrying the genetic heritage of Typhon and the woman behind Kypris. On this reading his enlightenment is partly orchestrated by Typhon within a closed, Gnostic system, yet it still serves the Outsider's will. The closing essay on "The Lost Pilgrim" reads it against Graves's Hercules, My Shipmate.

ti: The Launching Pad
sum: An editorial column by T.D.C. (presumably Thomas D. Clareson) on the state of academic criticism of science fiction and fantasy. It argues that recent literary criticism has turned inward into opaque jargon, partly from a desire for academic respectability. It also notes cooling enthusiasm for popular-culture studies, budget retreats and shifting canons. Wolfe appears briefly as the only reader who answered an earlier question about A. Merritt, and his Australian guest-of-honour speech is cited for criticizing how fantastic literature is taught. The column closes with proposed assumptions about two equal narrative traditions and fiction's inability…

ti: Wolfe Trap
sum: A review of Peter Wright's Attending Daedalus: Gene Wolfe, Artifice and the Reader (2003). The reviewer welcomes a long-overdue serious study, praising its clear writing, useful plot summaries of the New Sun cycle and its secondary bibliography, but rejects all three of Wright's theses: that Wolfe deliberately obfuscates his meaning, that his work centres on the biological imperative of genetic transmission, and that his post-New Sun fiction merely glosses that theme. The reviewer faults the reliance on authorial intent and the reduction of spiritual themes. Verdict: flawed but useful.

ti: Towards a Definition of Science Fantasy
sum: Malmgren proposes a definition of science fantasy as an unstable hybrid of SF and fantasy. Such a world contains at least one deliberate violation of natural law or empirical fact, yet supplies a scientific or quasi-scientific rationale and grounds its discourse in a scientific episteme. He reads Leiber's Conjure Wife and Lem's The Investigation as meta-texts that test the boundaries between science and magic. He then sorts the form into four types: time-loop, alternate present, counterscientific world and hybridized world. He argues that science fantasy questions scientific assumptions while exploring the reality of dream-world fears…

v: The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction
sum: Killheffer reviews Return to the Whorl, the concluding volume of The Book of the Short Sun, and praises it as a near-perfect end to a near-perfect epic, possibly Wolfe's best work. He summarizes Horn's Odyssey-like quest for Silk and stresses the after-the-fact, fragmentary narration, which he compares to Peace and the Latro books. He compares the novel's density to DeLillo's Underworld and places Wolfe's prose with Melville and Nabokov. He also discusses Horn's love for the inhumi and the overt Catholic and Eucharistic themes. His verdict is that it is a lesser sf novel than…

ti: Wolfe in the Fold
sum: Paul Kincaid reviews Peter Wright's edited volume Shadows of the New Sun: Wolfe on Writing/Writers on Wolfe (2007). He argues the subtitle misleads: there are no critical essays about Wolfe, and most of the book is fourteen reprinted interviews from 1973 to 2003. These repeat anecdotes and topics, dwell on Fifth Head and the New Sun, and neglect the comic and minor novels. He singles out the Brendan Baber interview and James B. Jordan's on Catholicism as valuable. Of Wolfe's short pieces, only the essay on the library books in Shadow impresses. Verdict: useful nuggets,…

A Books column in which Sallis reviews The Land Across alongside Pablo Capanna's study of Cordwainer Smith, framing both writers as singular mavericks within science fiction. He argues Wolfe fulfils rather than transcends genre traditions, praises "Forlesen" and Peace as quintessential Wolfe, and describes The Land Across as a Kafkaesque, dreamlike tale whose passive, shape-shifting narrator Grafton mirrors the novel's own mutability, with its ending reducing mystery to travelogue. The verdict is strongly positive. The Capanna book gets warm but qualified praise, faulted for trying to lift Smith out of the genre.

ti: The Wolf in the Labyrinth
sum: Swanwick's introductory appreciation, written to accompany Wolfe's story "Memorare" in the same magazine issue, argues against treating Wolfe as too lofty for ordinary readers. He reads "A Solar Labyrinth" as a seemingly light piece with darkening depths. He warns that critics hunting sources in The Wizard Knight overlook its central question of what makes a good knight. He ties Wolfe's moral ambiguity to his Catholicism and offers three rules for reading him. He also proposes that the women in "Memorare" are aspects of one woman.

ti: Lake of the Long Sun by Gene Wolfe
v: The New York Review of Science Fiction
sum: Thomas reviews the second Long Sun volume as a provisional report on a series still in progress. He outlines the Whorl as a generation ship with Roman-flavored culture and recaps Silk's plot with Chenille and the blackmail of Doctor Crane. He argues the series is unambiguously science fiction, unlike the New Sun's opening, while noting parallels between Silk and Severian and muted Christian allusion. Most attention goes to Wolfe's differentiated speech, especially Oreb's clipped utterances and Chenille's possessions, and to hidden clues that demand rereading. Verdict: highly favorable, with a mild complaint about self-conscious language.
